paragraphs: Rav Adda bar Ahavah. (1) Chapter Asarah Yuchasin 72, beginning of b: on the day Rabbi died he said prophetically, “Today Rav Adda bar Ahavah sits in our father Abraham’s bosom, peace be upon him.” Some explain that Rav Adda bar Ahavah died that day; if so, this is not the Rav Adda bar Ahavah of the Talmud. It appears that “sits in our father Abraham’s bosom” means he entered the covenant of circumcision. This is the very long-lived Rav Adda bar Ahavah (about 140 years; Shalshelet Hakkabbalah, folio 30), from Rabbi’s death to the later generations, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak’s days, as Bava Batra 22 says. End of Rashi. Likewise Bereshit Rabbah, Chayyei Sarah, beginning of section 58: on the day Rabbi died Rav Adda bar Ahavah was born (see Kohelet). Ta'anit, chapter 3, 20b: Rav and Shmuel would not pass under a precarious wall in Nehardea. One day Rav Adda bar Ahavah was there. Shmuel said to Rav, “Let the master come and go around.” He replied, “Not needed today: Rav Adda bar Ahavah is with us, his merit is great, and I am not afraid.” Rav Huna had wine in a precarious house and wished to remove it. He brought Rav Adda bar Ahavah inside and drew him into a discussion there until he had cleared it. After they left, the house fell. Rav Adda bar Ahavah realized and became angry, since one must not rely on a miracle, etc. What were his deeds? His students asked him (chapter Benei Ha'ir has Rabbi Zeira; some say Rav Adda bar Ahavah), “Through what have you lived long?” He replied, “I never grew angry in my home; never stepped before one greater in wisdom; never pondered in filthy alleys; never walked four cubits without Torah and tefillin; never slept in the study hall, even briefly; never rejoiced at a colleague’s mishap; never called a colleague by his chakhinah”—some say chanikhah (see Rashi and the Arukh). Jerusalem Talmud, end of Ta'anit, chapter 3, adds: “No one ever preceded me to the synagogue; I never left someone there and departed; my colleague’s curse never came onto my bed.” (Perhaps this means he forgave one who distressed him before sleep, like Mar Zutra, Megillah 28a.) “I did not walk in the marketplace beside someone indebted.” Berakhot 20a: he risked himself for sanctification of the Name by tearing a karbalta from a Kuti woman, thinking her Jewish, because it was mixed wool and linen. Rabbi Tzemach Gaon explains it was immodest clothing such as Jewish women do not wear. He had to pay 400 zuz. Asking her name, she said Matun. He told her, “Matun, matun”—deliberation—“is worth 400 zuz.” Bava Batra, chapter 2, 22a: Rav Dimi of Nehardea brought dried figs by boat. The exilarch told Rava, “See whether he is a scholar; if so, reserve the market for him.” Rava told Rav Adda bar Ahavah to test him. He asked: an elephant swallowed an Egyptian basket and expelled it through its rectum—what is its status? (Is it digested, like a dung vessel, and not susceptible to impurity?) He did not know. He asked, “Are you Rava?” (He had heard Rava was the city’s great man and thought this was he.) He replied, “Much separates me from Rava; nevertheless, I am your master, and Rava your master’s master.” They did not reserve the market; his figs were lost. He came to Rav Yosef: “See what he did to me.” Rav Yosef said, “May the One who did not delay the wrong done to Edom’s king not delay your wrong,” etc. Rav Adda bar Ahavah died. Rav Yosef said, “I punished him: I cursed him.” Rav Dimi: “I did, for he ruined my figs.” Abaye: “I did, for he said to the rabbis, Instead of gnawing bones at Abaye’s, eat meat at Rava’s” (see there). Rava: “I did, for he told the butchers, I take meat before Rava’s attendant”—his emissary to buy meat—“because I am better than he.” Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: “I did.” He was head of the kallah, expounding publicly on Shabbat. Every day before entering, he reviewed his teaching with Rav Adda bar Ahavah, then entered. That day Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua detained Rav Adda bar Ahavah, since they had not been at the conclusion. (They had not been in the council appointing Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak; some explain they missed the conclusion of Rava’s festival-Shabbat lecture.) They asked, “Tell us those teachings—how did Rava say them?” He answered, “Thus said Rava.” Meanwhile it grew late and he had not come. The rabbis told Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, “Get up: it is late! Why does the master sit?” He replied, “I sit waiting for Rav Adda bar Ahavah’s bier.” Word then came that he had died. It is reasonable that Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak punished him. End quotation. Yuchasin writes that responsa Rivash, section 17, explains each man’s “I punished him” as grief that he was punished on his account: “Punishing even the righteous is not good.” (It is surprising he did not see Tosafot say this.) Tosafot there, 22a: R.Ch. does not read that Rava sent Rav Adda bar Ahavah, but Rav Adda bar Abba, since Rav Adda bar Ahavah was in Rabbi’s time. End quotation. Yet the Arukh, entry T.H., has our reading: Rava sent Rav Adda bar Ahavah.

(2) Yuchasin writes that there were two Rav Adda bar Ahavahs, as Tosafot state in Asarah Yuchasin 72b, Ta'anit 20a, Avodah Zarah 35a; see there. One was Rav and Shmuel’s colleague, another Rava’s student. Panim Masbirot supports Tosafot: Berakhot 20a has Abaye say, “The earlier ones risked their lives for sanctification of the Name,” such as Rav Adda bar Ahavah above; thus he preceded Abaye. Yet Bava Batra has him say, “Instead of gnawing bones at Abaye’s,” etc., implying he lived in Abaye’s days. (Niddah, chapter 3, 23a: he asked Abaye.) This proves there were two, as Tosafot say. End quotation. Given his longevity above, calling him “earlier” proves nothing. Tosafot, Avodah Zarah 35a: this is not Rava’s student, since his words are mentioned before those of Rav Chisda and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, who preceded Rava. End quotation. This requires examination: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak was Rava’s student. How could they place him before Rava, or before Rav Chisda, Rava’s teacher, even though he lived long? Yuchasin compels the two-person distinction with powerful arguments: Rav Adda bar Ahavah was Rava’s student, arranging his teaching twenty-four times before entering before Rava, Ta'anit 8a; speaking in Rava’s name, Pesachim 14a; speaking to Rava, Makkot 8a; Yoma 14, beginning of a, “Did Rabbi Yehudah say so?”; Shabbat 94a; Yoma 73a; likewise Bava Batra above, “Much separates me from Rava,” despite claiming meat before Rava’s attendant. The last chapter of Ta'anit (it should be chapter 3) places him in Rav and Shmuel’s time. Berakhot 42b: Rav’s student, present at Rav’s burial and tearing his garment. Makkot 23b: he spoke in Rav’s name; Eruvin 7a; Beitzah 13, end of b; Ketubbot 24a; Jerusalem Talmud, Shor Shenagach Arba'ah Vachamishah, halakhah 2: present when Rav said, etc. Keritot 15: Rav said in his name. How could this man be among the later ones? Not merely because of the many years, more than 140. (That means from Rabbi’s death and Rav Adda bar Ahavah’s birth until his death in Rava’s generation. But this is incorrect: according to Raavad Rabbi died in 3948, Rav Yosef in 4085, and Rav Yosef was still alive when Rav Adda bar Ahavah died, as in Bava Batra above. Only 137 years separate his birth from Rav Yosef’s death; Rav Yosef may have lived some years after him. Certainly, if Rabbi died in 3979, Rav Yosef’s death would be no more than 106 years later.) Rather, how could Rava, still young while his teacher Rav Yosef lived—not more than thirty—treat him as a student and send him to test Rav Dimi, when Rav and Shmuel honored him? Rava was born when Rav Yehudah died, in 4060; Rav Yosef died in 4085, so Rava was twenty-five at Rav Yosef’s death, and not even twenty-five while he lived. How could Rav Dimi ask whether he was Rava, failing to distinguish a young man from a 140-year-old? All the more since he called Rava his teacher and reported Rava’s teachings to Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua and Rav Pappa. Could one whose protection Rav and Shmuel relied on, saying “We shall live in his shade,” a hundred years later be disparaged as inferior to Rava’s servant buying his master’s meat, and Rava say he punished him for it? In Haba Al Yevimto 61b Rava calls him one lacking sense; in Ellu Hannisrafin 81, beginning of b, “my son”—would he address an aged holy sage thus? Shabbat 140a: Rav Adda bar Ahavah was teacher to the elderly Rav Acha bar Yosef, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak’s uncle. Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin tells Rav Acha b.Y., “I asked your teacher” (our reading omits “your teacher”), “Rav Adda bar Ahavah and Rav Huna.” Makkot, chapter Ellu Hen Hallokin (I did not find it there), Merubbeh 81, end of a, and Shenei Nezirim 57b suggest he died before Rav Huna: throughout his life Rav Huna had no surviving children, like Shmuel throughout Rav’s life (see there). As Rav died before Shmuel’s children survived, so Rav Adda bar Ahavah must have died before Rav Huna’s children survived. Then he died before Rav Huna, who died before Rav Yehudah, when Rava was born; the man dying in Rava’s days must therefore be another. Yet see what I wrote under Rav Huna: Rav Huna died first. That is also compelled by the dates: Rav Huna died in 4050; if Rabbi died in 3979, only seventy-one years passed. If Rav Adda bar Ahavah died earlier still, allowing surviving offspring for Rav Huna, he would not even have lived the ordinary seventy years. Why ask how he lived long? Necessarily Rav Huna died first and Rav Adda bar Ahavah was old. On “Throughout Rav Adda bar Ahavah’s years none survived,” see Rav Huna.

Tosafot, Ta'anit 20b, write that there were two: he was Rav and Shmuel’s colleague, as they said, “Rav Adda bar Ahavah is with us”; Rav Yehudah was Rav’s student, Rava was born when Rav Yehudah died, and Rav Adda bar Ahavah was Rava’s student. End quotation. They resorted to this despite his longevity: he could have lived until punished over Rav Dimi’s figs. But Rava sent him to test Rav Dimi like a master sending a student. How could Rav and Shmuel’s colleague be the student of Rav’s student’s student? Thus the punished man was a second Rav Adda bar Ahavah. Moreover, if the early man was punished in that incident, he was old: who told them death was punishment, rather than natural? Necessarily the punished man was young, hence they attributed his punishment to themselves. (Tosafot seek a repair through R.Ch.’s reading: Rava sent Rav Adda bar Abba, who lived in Rava’s time as I shall write below, since Rav Adda bar Ahavah lived in Rabbi’s time. End quotation. Emendation is not compelled: “in Rabbi’s time” means born when Rabbi died, and longevity could reach Rava’s time. Moreover, even correcting Bava Batra leaves Rav Adda bar Ahavah as Rava’s student, reviewing twenty-four times before entering, and reporting Rava many times. It is hard to change Ahavah to Abba everywhere; he also occurs repeatedly with Rava’s colleague Abaye above. R.Ch.’s change to Abba was therefore needless: “Many waters cannot quench Ahavah”—love.)

The compelling difficulties suggest the man dying in Rava’s time was the second, not the elder with Rav and Shmuel, whose merit they relied on in Ta'anit and whose long life they asked about. Another compelling proof: Kiddushin 54b and Bava Kamma 24a have Rav Nachman speaking in Rav Adda bar Ahavah’s name; this suggests he was Rav Nachman’s teacher (see the introductory rules). Yevamot 110b: Rav Nachman found him and his son-in-law Rav Chanan gathering gatherings in Pumbedita’s marketplace. Rashi: gathering students to hear their words; another explanation, answering each other’s objections. Since Rav Nachman appears his student, and Tosafot, Avodah Zarah 58a, call Rava Rav Nachman’s student (see there), how could he be his student’s student? Bava Kamma 24a conversely has him speaking in Rav Nachman’s name, suggesting Rav Nachman was his teacher. One may answer that the second Rav Adda bar Ahavah was a student of Rav Nachman and Rava, or invoke the rule that a master can report his student. Chagigah 25a: he spoke to Rav Nachman.

(3) Yet I question whether two suffice: it is almost necessary to posit three. Chullin 133b: he explained it before Rav Pappa. Tosafot, Shabbat 93a, say Rav Pappa was Rava’s student; Rava became academy head after Rav Yosef’s death, Rav Pappa after Rava’s. If the second died while Rav Yosef lived, this speaker before Rav Pappa must be the long-lived first, born at Rabbi’s death, then 165 years old or more (see part I; examine and find). How could a 165-year-old interpret before Rav Pappa? More puzzling: Yevamot 87a, “Rav Adda bar Ahavah said: It was taught, When she returns to her father’s house,” etc. Rav Mordekhai reported it before Rav Ashi, who asked, “Whence?”, etc. Asarah Yuchasin says Rav Ashi was born when Rava died; he became academy head in 4127, and Rabbi died in 3948. Thus the first Rav Adda bar Ahavah would be approximately 185 years or more.

(4) Shabbat 135a: Rav Adda bar Ahavah had a son born circumcised. He brought him around to thirteen circumcisers to draw covenantal blood, but they refused because it was Shabbat. He circumcised him himself and left him with a severed reproductive passage [כרות שפכה], saying, “May it come upon me, for I transgressed Rav’s ruling.” On the day he died, his son Rav Hamnuna was born (Midrash Kohelet on “The sun rises and the sun sets”; Bereshit Rabbah, Chayyei Sarah, differs). He was more exact than Shmuel in the science of the solar seasons: we rely on him in leap years, “Observe the month of spring,” so that the Omer day is properly in the spring season. Shmuel’s cycle leaves an hour and 485 parts. He divided this among the seventy-six seasons in the cycle; each part he divided into seventy-six secondary parts, called moments. Each season’s share was twenty parts and forty-five moments. A mnemonic: if asked how much the excess is—kamah—reply that the question is its answer: כ׳ parts, מ״ה moments. According to his calculation, the solar and lunar years end each cycle exactly together, without a moment of excess or deficiency (see Tzemach David). At the end of Yevamot he praised Rava as sharper than Abaye. He erred: Yevamot 122, beginning of a, has a woman before Abaye (see there), delayed three festivals. Rav Adda bar Ahavah told her, “Go to Rav Yosef, whose knife is sharp.” Perhaps the error came from Rabbi Adda bar Machana praising Rava’s sharp knife against Abaye, Chullin 77a; see Abaye. Or from Bava Batra above: “Instead of gnawing bones at Abaye’s, eat meat at Rava’s.”

(5) He spoke to Rabbi Abba bar Zavda. See Rav Acha. Rav Idi bar Gershon in his name; he spoke to Rabbi Assi. Rav Bibi in his name; Rav Hamnuna before him; Rav Hamnuna the elder in his name; Rabbi Ze'ira in his name. Rabbi Chana, his son-in-law (see above). Rav Chuna in his name; Rabbi Chanina bar Avdimi; Rabbi Chanina bar Idi asked him. Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha; Rabbi Yirmeyah. Rav Malkiyo in his name, and in R. Malkiyo’s name; Rav Malkiyah in his name. Rav Nachman in his name, and he in Rav Nachman’s name (see above). Mar, his son—requires examination. Rav, his teacher; Rava, his teacher; Shmuel; Rabbi Shmuel bar Chalafta.
